passage:
In 1933, the country was deep in the Great Depression. President Roosevelt started the Civilian Conservation Corps to give young men work outdoors. By May, two CCC camps stood in the Shenandoah Valley, at Skyland and at Big Meadows, and more than 1,000 young men lived in them. The Army ran the camps, and the National Park Service chose the work. The park itself did not exist yet, because it would not open until 1935. Roosevelt wanted the camps seen, so photographers followed his tour. Between 1933 and 1942, ten CCC camps were set up in or near the park. Most early work stayed along the narrow strip of land beside the road.

The men built the park from the ground up, and their projects fell into three groups: buildings, roads and trails, and landscaping. They cut trails and fire roads, put up log comfort stations, and cleared picnic grounds. They built a sawmill and cut lumber for park buildings, and some of the lumber came from chestnut trees that a blight had killed years earlier. A shingle mill made heavy tiles shaped like wood shingles. A blacksmith shop made hinges, latches, and tools. Workers raised plants in nurseries, so bare ground could be planted again. A sign shop made wooden signboards for the park.

The crews did more than build. They also changed how the land looked. They removed dead chestnut trees, thinned the undergrowth, and cut deadwood to lower the risk of fire. They planted trees, shrubs, and small plants along the road, and they spent eight years trying to remove an invasive tree called Ailanthus. A landscape architect named Benson planned the views. Researchers now say that no area in view of the Skyline Drive is fully natural. The land was shaped on purpose, for the eye of a driver. Visitors see a park that looks wild, but people made it that way.

key.confirm: Right. Crews cleared, planted, and shaped the land to create those views.
key.tell: Because people cleared, planted, and shaped the land to make the views along the road.

passage:
Crates of apples arrive at the packing shed and are tipped into a tank of water. The water floats the fruit onto a belt and carries it under a first spray. From there the apples climb a ramp to the sizer, which drops each one into a lane by size. The smallest apples fall first, and the largest ride to the far end of the sizer. A boxer at each lane packs the fruit and stacks the box on a pallet. The line runs from the dump tank to the pallet without stopping, and every step waits for the step before it.

The wash belt was the slow step, so the crew added a second belt and doubled the spray. The wash now moves fruit faster than the sizer can grade it. The pile did not go away. It moved down the line and collected in front of the sizer, where the apples roll against each other and bruise. The crew had spent a week and a good deal of money on a step that was not holding the line back. Output stayed the same, and the fruit that waited at the sizer sat longer in the water. The shed manager walked the line at noon and found the pile in the same place it had always been.

The line moves at the speed of its slowest step, so speeding up another step adds waiting room, not boxes. The sizer cannot be widened, because each size needs its own lane and each lane needs its own boxer. So the crew added a second boxer to the lane that filled fastest and moved the staff from the wash. The pile shifted again, this time to the boxers. The wash had been fine all along. A crew that fixes the wrong station pays twice, once for the change and once for the fruit that waits. The only way to find the slow step is to watch where the fruit collects.

passage:
In buying flour, whether bread or pastry, select the best kept by your grocer. Bread flour should be used in all cases where yeast is called for, with few exceptions; in other cases, pastry flour. The difference between bread and pastry flour may be readily determined. Take bread flour in the hand, close hand tightly, then open. Flour will not keep in shape; if allowed to pass through fingers it will feel slightly granular. Take pastry flour in the hand, close hand tightly, open, and flour will be in shape, having impression of the lines of the hand, and feeling soft and velvety to touch. Flour should always be sifted before measuring.

Yeast is a tiny plant. It is a fungus. It is the lowest form of plant life; these spores grow by budding and division; they multiply fast in good conditions. They make fermentation. Fermentation is how sugar turns into alcohol and carbon dioxide. Air, warmth, moisture, and a ferment cause this; when bread dough ferments with yeast, the fermentation is alcoholic; if alcoholic fermentation goes on too long, acetic fermentation starts; acetic fermentation follows alcoholic. Lactic fermentation happens when milk sours. Compressed yeast cakes in tinfoil have long worked well. They are now almost always used. They have replaced home-made liquid yeast; never use a yeast cake unless it is perfectly fresh; you can tell by its light color and lack of dark streaks. The yeast plant is killed at 212° F; at 32° F, life is paused but not fully destroyed.

The best temperature for its growth is 65° to 68° F. Fermented bread is made by mixing flour into a dough with a definite quantity of water, milk, or water and milk, salt, and a ferment. Sugar is usually added to hasten fermentation. Knead the dough so the ingredients are thoroughly incorporated. Cover it and let it rise at 68° F. until it has doubled its bulk. Knead the dough a second time to break bubbles and distribute the carbon dioxide evenly. Shape it into loaves and put them in greased bread pans, half filled. Cover them and let them rise at the same temperature as the first rising, until they double their bulk. If risen too long, it will be full of large holes; if not risen long enough, it will be heavy and soggy.
